mcqs.question: Why does the scheduler use a min-heap ordered by next-fire-time instead of scanning a plain list of all scheduled tasks?
options: Because a plain list cannot store objects of different task types
Because the heap prevents any task from ever being cancelled
Because Trigger implementations require a heap-based data structure to compute the next fire time
Finding the task due soonest is O(1) with a min-heap, since it's always at the top, instead of scanning every task on every tick
mcqs.explanation: The min-heap's whole value is keeping the earliest deadline instantly accessible, so the scheduler never scans the full task set to find what's next. Plain lists can store any object type, tasks can still be cancelled with a heap in use, and a Trigger's job is unrelated to the container structure holding tasks.

mcqs.question: In the reschedule logic, what does the overrun policy decide?
options: Whether a task that took longer than its interval fires again immediately to catch up, or skips ahead to its next regular interval boundary
Whether the task is removed from the scheduler permanently after overrunning once
Whether the task runs on the loop thread or a separate worker thread
Whether the min-heap needs to be rebuilt from scratch after an overrun
mcqs.explanation: The overrun policy specifically governs the choice between catching up immediately or skipping to the next regular boundary when a task ran longer than its own interval. It doesn't remove the task, doesn't decide thread placement — that's a separate execution-isolation concern — and doesn't require rebuilding the heap.

mcqs.question: Why does running each due task on a separate worker thread pool, rather than directly on the scheduler's loop thread, matter?
options: It's required because tasks cannot execute on the same thread as a priority queue
It keeps the scheduling decision — what's next and when — completely decoupled from how long any individual task takes, so one hung task can't block delivery to every other scheduled task
It makes the min-heap operations run in constant time instead of logarithmic time
It removes the need for a Trigger implementation on any task
mcqs.explanation: Offloading execution to a worker pool means the loop thread's only job — deciding what's next — never gets stuck behind a slow or hung task's actual execution. There's no such thread/data-structure restriction, worker pools don't change the heap's algorithmic complexity, and every task still needs a Trigger regardless of where it executes.

mcqs.question: What's the actual risk of running every scheduled task directly on the scheduler's own loop thread with no isolation?
options: The min-heap would need to be replaced with a different data structure
Tasks would no longer be able to access their Trigger's next-fire-time calculation
A single task that runs long, hangs, or throws blocks or kills the one thread responsible for scheduling every other task too
It's actually a safe and recommended design as long as tasks are short
mcqs.explanation: Because the loop thread is the only thing deciding what runs next, tying task execution to that same thread means one bad task degrades the entire scheduler, not just itself. The heap and Trigger calculations are unaffected either way, and this remains risky even for typically-short tasks, since any one of them can misbehave unexpectedly.
